Tutu Tribute

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Reflecting on Desmond Tutu's contribution to South Africa's democracy

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews with people who have shared close relationship with Archbishop Emeritus Desmond Tutu, who will reflect on his spirituality, values and legacy in the country and globally.


Summary:
At 90 years old Desmond Tutu remains a revered figure in the country, celebrated across races and faiths, for his advocacy and cause for a just and inclusive society.

Script:


The apartheid government and its machinery had to contend with this firey preacher. Desmond Mpilo Tutu, Defiant and steadfast in the face of repression.

In the 70s and 80s the regime was unrepentant. The church became the cornerstone of the townships. The South African Council Of Churches and clerics like Tutu, Father Smangaliso Mkhatshwa, Beyers Naude and Father Trevor Huddleston, engaged the church in social justice issues.


As the Dean of Johannesburg, living in Soweto at the time, could sense and feel the growing discontent and the rising anger.


Reverend Barney Pityana, is an activists and one of Tutu’s former theology student.

Barney Pityana

CLIP2 - 2DK00
00;15 - 00;44
‘Barely a month the youth uprisings happened’


Tutu’s premonition. The 1976 student uprisings saw many students detained, some escaped to exile and scores killed.

As the Secretary General of the SACC, his work as an activist became prominent. Black movements were banned and political leaders were in Robben Island.

Barney Pityana
02;53 - 03;58
‘One fo the key things as general secretary….
Zaki Achmat was a political activist in the 80s and would later lend his voice to social justice issues and the equality of LGBTQI peoples


Dr Brigalia Bam, a close family friend and colleague for many decades.


Zaki Achmat
00;43 - 01;31


Brigalia Bam
10;13 - 10;46
To be able to be with families…




In the fury of angry crowds, at rallies and funerals, his empathy and compassion brought comfort.


Brigalia Bam

13;03 - 13;46

BP
50Y00 – clip6
00;19 – 00;56 Barney ‘ and he was in the forefront, of all of those whenever there was fighting, rioting, necklacing, and killing and informers, and impipis, he was there at funeral when people were about to be killed. He put his body on the line in order to prevent the outflowing of the angger of the people in the communities. But all of that was in the context of being a church person , either general council of churches, or archbishop of cape town or bishop of johannesburg’

Chris Ahrends

-01:29 - 01:44 01:59 - 02:12


In his cassock or robes, he was a preacher who spoke truth to power. Unflinching in his rebuke of the National Party government.



After just a few months in office in 1989, former apartheid President FW de Klerk found himself in one of Tutu’s admonishing rebukes.


Brigalia Bam
04:39 and then he switches to English, he says to mr de klerk tell me on a personal level, when you go to bed, at the end of the day, do you feel so good about all the people who go to bed without food, how do you feel about those people who are in Robben island who are away from their families… 05; 28 and all those people who are tortured, and desmond goes slowly and de klerk is listening, attentively. I was probably more tense, I was ready to die, I’m sitting this side and no one is expecting this kind of, this is now, the meeting is over. 06; 44 You know I have never forgotten this conversation, never 06;51 AND DE KLERK says, not looking angry at all, looking very sober, and he says of you are talking in that way, in that style of talking, I am going to tell you the truth, I am also speaking to you as a human being not, as a head of state. 07:23 and says to desmond we are afraid.


The archbishop’s voice continued to reverberate, calling for freedom and democracy.


CITY HALL viz of Mandela….celebration voice underneath


Even in democratic South Africa, Tutu’s voice remained prominent in issues of social justice, he’d also rebuke the ANC government for its failures.
In 1997, Tutu sat down with Carte Blanche, on his reflections of the country at the time.

Tutu Conversations - Ruda Int

Tutu 02:21 - 02:35
“It is also good for us to remember that there is no guarantee that those who were yesterday’s oppressed, would not become tomorrow’s oppressors.
It was during the Truth and Reconciliation Commission where the world saw his deep sense of empathy. Hearing testimonies, from survivors, and loved ones of victims of torture, detention and harrasment at the hands of apartheid police.

Tutu Conversations - Ruda Int
04;42 - 05;18 - i try not to cry because if i break down then attention is diverted to me


Tutu carried these people and their pain in his heart, and prayer, through these kind of difficult moments was his solace and reprieve.



Chris
00;02 - 01;34


A symbol of forgiveness and reconciliation, Tutu represented these values for a once segregated society, when envisioned a new South Africa, a rainbow nation.


Brigalia
12;17 - 13;00 13;04 ‘these people who mean it and are for real and they mean it
13;22 - 13;34
In his later years, Tutu continued in his advocacy work, lending his voice to advance the causes of the marginalised.

A global guiding light for peace, devoted to his faith and the people.


Zaki
2;18 Because I’ve been involved in political struggles and subsequently Ive been in the struggle for gay and lesbian equality, the arch was supportive for the equality of gay and lesbian people at the time and to this. day he remains an ardent supporter of GLBTQ and Intersexed people
